mechanism.one_line: Rank by bid x predicted click-through rate; charge the minimum needed to hold position, quality-adjusted; let anyone in for five dollars.

formal.name: Quality-weighted generalized second-price (AdWords Select, deployed 2002-2008)
formal.players: Advertisers bidding a maximum CPC; Google, which also estimates the quality weight, validates the click and bills the log; searchers.
formal.strategies: Choose a max CPC per keyword. Bids and quality scores are private. From 2004 a bid-management industry (iProspect, Did-It, Performics, Efficient Frontier) sold strategy as a service.
formal.allocation_rule: AdRank = bid x predicted click-through rate. Sort by AdRank, descending. This is a ranking by expected revenue per impression, not by willingness to pay.
formal.payment_rule: Winner in slot j pays the minimum needed to hold position, quality-adjusted: p_j = (b_(j+1) * q_(j+1)) / q_j + $0.01, charged per click, capped at its own max CPC. The last slot pays the reserve.

deployed_divergences_from_textbook_gsp: The one-cent increment: prices are next-AdRank plus a fixed increment, not exactly next-AdRank.

mechanism.the_reframe: AdRank is not a relevance filter with a revenue side effect. pure_bid.payment_rule: Winner in slot j pays the bid of the advertiser in slot j+1, plus one cent. Charged per click.

first_price_shading.name: Unified first-price auction with equilibrium bid shading (Google Ad Manager display exchange, from 2019-09-05)
first_price_shading.players: Demand-side platforms and exchanges bidding on behalf of advertisers; publishers setting unified pricing rules; Google operating both the exchange and the publisher ad server.
first_price_shading.strategies: Bid a shaded value: b(v) = v * (n-1)/n in the symmetric benchmark, or in practice the output of a proprietary bid-shading model estimating the clearing price.
first_price_shading.allocation_rule: Highest bid wins (quality-weighted equivalents apply where a quality term exists).
first_price_shading.information: The clearing price is set by the buyer's own model rather than by the runner-up's bid. Google committed to bid data files for publishers and post-auction feedback for buyers as part of the change.
first_price_shading.objective_maximised: Nothing new. Under symmetry, IPV and risk neutrality this is revenue-equivalent to second price for every n - see ex-4.
first_price_shading.why_it_happened: Header bidding (2014-15, standardised by Prebid.js) made publishers compare a first-price header bid against a second-price exchange result run by their own ad server. First price plus unified pricing rules made the comparison apples-to-apples. Google's own stated finding was that first-price auctions have a 'neutral to positive impact on a publisher's total revenue' - a transparency and competitive-pressure change, not a yield change.
first_price_shading.scope_warning: THIS WAS DISPLAY, NOT SEARCH. Google Search never moved to first price. The 2019 search-side change was rGSP, which the DOJ record shows was an explicit revenue play. Conflating the two is the standard error in retellings of the 2019 transition.

vcg_benchmark.name: Vickrey-Clarke-Groves position auction (truthful benchmark, never deployed on search)
vcg_benchmark.allocation_rule: Same efficient allocation as quality-weighted GSP: sort by bid x quality.
vcg_benchmark.payment_rule: Each winner pays the externality it imposes on the others: the sum over lower positions of (click difference) x (displaced bidder's value).
vcg_benchmark.property: Truthful bidding is a dominant strategy, so the mechanism's revenue is a determinate number rather than a band.
vcg_benchmark.why_it_matters_here: VCG is the yardstick that turns 'GSP is not truthful' from an adjective into arithmetic. In ex-2/ex-3 VCG revenue is $440, exactly the lowest locally-envy-free GSP equilibrium; naive truthful play under GSP yields $760. The difference between those two numbers is the value of advertiser sophistication, and it is 73% of the floor.

gsp_not_truthful.summary: With slot click volumes of 100 and 80 and values of $10, $6 and $2, the top bidder earns $400 by bidding its value and $640 by bidding $5. The deviation survives the one-cent increment ($399 vs $639.20) and survives quality weighting, because a common quality divisor rescales both sides of the comparison equally. GSP's payment rule ties your price to the bid below you, so buying a worse slot buys a cheaper price - the exact trade VCG closes and GSP leaves open.
gsp_not_truthful.consequence_for_the_other_claims: GSP revenue is a band, not a number: [$440 lowest locally-envy-free equilibrium = VCG revenue, $760 naive truthful play], a 1.727x spread. Claims C2 and C3 are proven at equal bids; the equilibrium correction runs in the advertisers' favour, and any simulator that shows truthful bidding overstates GSP revenue by up to 73%.

rgsp_coda.verdict: DEMONSTRATED for all three knobs; squashing's exponent is assumed because it has never been disclosed.
rgsp_coda.thesis: By 2019 the mechanism was no longer doing the pricing. Three named knobs were, and each one moves price with quality, allocation and creative held fixed.

knobs.what_it_does: Ranks and prices on b * q^gamma with gamma < 1, compressing the quality dimension so the winner's price rises toward the runner-up's raw bid.
knobs.worked_result: Markup = (q_next/q_own)^(gamma-1). At gamma = 0.95026 on a 0.03/0.08 quality gap the markup is exactly +5%, matching Dischler's disclosed average. At gamma = 0.5 on the ex-1 cast it restores the PURE-BID ranking - 18 clicks per 1000 impressions instead of 58 - while collecting 45.3% more total revenue than pure-bid ever did for that same worse allocation.
knobs.parameter_status: assumed - not in the public record

knobs.what_it_does: Applies a separate price multiplier to ad formats. No ranking change.
knobs.worked_result: A 20% share of observed RPM implies a 25% uplift on the counterfactual base; at the disclosed +15% per launch with about half retained, three launches compound to +24.2%, so the disclosed share is roughly three launches deep. At 2008 revenue levels a 20% RPM knob is worth $4,226m - 42% of the entire US newspaper classified market that year.
knobs.parameter_status: disclosed in the Mehta findings of fact

knobs.what_it_does: Randomises the ordering of similarly-scored ads so a lower-Ad-Rank ad can appear above a higher one, breaking the reliability of the bid-down-a-slot trade that makes shading profitable under plain GSP. Advertisers cannot opt out.
knobs.worked_result: Disclosed +5.91% top-slot CPC on PC/tablet and +4.85% on mobile in pre-launch tests, 40-50% stickage, +5.74% revenue persisting two months post-launch. Placed against the ex-3 equilibrium band, +5.74% traverses only 7.9% of the distance from the lowest equilibrium to naive truthful play. The knob did not have to be big, because GSP's own band is 73% wide and the seller sits on it.
knobs.parameter_status: magnitudes disclosed; the pricing rule itself is not public

rgsp_coda.continuity_finding: The knobs are not a break with the 2002-2008 mechanism. The reserve-price channel was already a direct seller-set price from August 2005 (quality-based minimum bids), and on a one-bidder query the reserve IS the price - see break-2, where moving the minimum bid from $0.01 to $1.00 changes revenue 100x with one advertiser, one ad and one user experience. What 2019 added was scale and a trial transcript.
rgsp_coda.open_tension: The record says rGSP replaced format pricing because rGSP made more money, yet format pricing was ~20% of text-ads RPM while rGSP's disclosed persistent revenue effect was +5.74%. Either the 20% was not all incremental, or the two knobs were substitutes extracting the same surplus. The record as summarised does not resolve this and this analysis does not assert a resolution.

breaks.statement: b x q maximises expected revenue per impression. Relevance improves only insofar as clicks proxy relevance, and click-through rate alone rewards whatever gets clicked, including ads that mislead. findings.text: Pure-bid ranking mis-orders by expected revenue exactly when 1 < b_i/b_j < q_j/q_i. In the worked case the bid ratio is 3 and the CTR ratio is 5, so the pure-bid order (Aster, Brindle, Cedar) is the precise reverse of the expected-revenue order.

Same example, both metrics: revenue per 1000 impressions rises from $28.18 to $52.58 (+86.6%) and clicks delivered rise from 18 to 58 (+222%). The two metrics move together because clicks are the currency of both sides.

The revenue gain is a VOLUME effect, not a price effect. Average price per click FALLS 42%, from $1.57 to $0.91. Pure-bid maximises willingness to pay per click; AdRank maximises revenue per impression, and impressions are the scarce good. Every retelling that describes quality-weighting as letting Google charge more has the sign backwards.

The gain survives only while the seller's click-through estimate is roughly right. At a predicted 5% against a true CTR under 1.99%, quality-weighting earns less than the crude design it replaced. No independent standard for counting a click existed until 2009 and no MRC accreditation of search click counting existed in period, so this parameter was unauditable throughout the era.

Both GSP winners pay below their bids ($0.81 against $1.00; $1.51 against $2.00) and the total is still 1.87x the pure-bid total. GSP collects 79.7% of what pay-your-bid would collect on the same bids and still beats pure-bid by 87%, because it is charging a smaller margin on a much larger click base.

GSP is not truthful: $400 truthful against $640 shaded, in a three-bidder two-slot example, robust to the one-cent increment and to quality weighting. Under VCG the same bidder earns $720 by telling the truth.

The consequence is that GSP revenue is a band of [$440, $760] - a factor of 1.727 - whose position depends on advertiser sophistication rather than on the mechanism. The lowest equilibrium is exactly VCG-revenue-equivalent. Any comparison holding bids fixed, including this analysis's own C1-C3 example, measures a point the bidders choose. A simulator that displays truthful bidding overstates GSP revenue by up to 73%.

First-price with equilibrium shading and second-price yield identical expected revenue for n = 2, 3, 5 and 10 - both collapse to V*(n-1)/(n+1). There is no yield mechanism in the first-price rule. The apparent 86% windfall from Google's own 10-K bid example ($2.10 versus $1.13) is entirely an artefact of freezing bids.

Equivalence needs symmetry, IPV, risk neutrality and a common reserve. Seller revenue is linear in the market's average shading factor, spanning -17.5% to +20% over a 0.55-0.80 range against an equilibrium 0.667. The 2019 change's real effect is that the clearing price moved from being computed by the seller's runner-up to being computed by the buyer's model - which is exactly the transparency argument, since the previous second-price computation was performed by a party that also intermediated the auction.

The two 2019 changes ran in opposite directions on opposite sides of the business: display went to unified first price on 2019-09-05 with a transparency rationale and a self-reported neutral-to-positive revenue effect, while search got rGSP with an explicit revenue rationale and a disclosed +5.74% persistent gain. Search never went first-price. This is the most common factual error in retellings of 2019 and the analysis must state it explicitly.

Each knob moves price with quality, allocation and creative held constant. Squashing at gamma = 0.95026 delivers exactly the +5% Dischler described on a 0.03/0.08 quality gap; at gamma = 0.5 on the era-6 cast it restores the pure-bid ranking (18 clicks instead of 58) while collecting 45.3% more than pure-bid. Format pricing's disclosed 20% RPM share is roughly three compounding launches of the disclosed size. rGSP's disclosed +5.74% traverses 7.9% of GSP's own equilibrium band.

The knobs did not have to be large, and they did not have to replace the auction. GSP already under-determined revenue by 73% because the payment depends on how well bidders play; the seller sits on that band and the knobs are instruments for moving the market inside it. The mechanism became a price-setting instrument by being tuned, not by being abandoned.

The pricing-knob story starts in era 6, not in 2019. From August 2005 Quality Score set per-keyword minimum bids, and on a one-bidder query the minimum bid IS the price - moving it from $0.01 to $1.00 is a 100x revenue change with one advertiser, one ad and no change to the user's experience. The seller has been setting prices directly on the long tail since three years before the era closed.

This analysis proves the design is better on the metric it optimises. It does not prove the design caused the capture. Overture ran the pure-bid auction and led paid-search revenue through 2002 ($667.7m against Google's $439.5m of total revenue); Yahoo adopted quality weighting only on 5 February 2007, five years late and long after the distribution war was settled. The auction explains yield per query; it does not explain query volume. Read this section against the distribution engine, not instead of it.

findings.text: Every parameter that decides who wins and what they pay - predicted click-through rate, the quality-based reserve, the squashing exponent, the format multiplier, the click validity test - was computed by the seller, undisclosed as a number, and unaudited by any third party. That is the same institutional fact in 2005 and in 2019. The mechanism-design case for the auction is sound; the governance case never existed.

mechanism.name: Search-advertising distribution: revenue-share syndication, minimum-revenue guarantees, and exclusive default placement (1998-2008, with a 2024 coda)
mechanism.one_line: A search engine buys query volume from whoever owns the user's starting point, paying a share of the advertising revenue those queries generate, sometimes floored by a guarantee and sometimes bought with equity, in exchange for default or exclusive placement.

actors.access_point_owner: AOL, Apple, Mozilla, Android OEMs, carriers, or any web publisher: owns the surface where a query begins. Sells placement, not inventory-quality.
actors.search_engine: Google or Overture: runs the auction that converts a query into revenue. Buys placement with a share of that revenue.
actors.advertiser: Bids in the search engine's auction. Never a party to the distribution contract, and in the syndicated case usually cannot see which surface the click came from.
actors.rival_search_engine: The bidder who loses the placement, and with it the queries.

mechanism.allocation_rule: The access-point owner allocates the default (and in the exclusive case, the only) slot to one search engine, typically by private negotiation shaped like a first-price sealed-bid auction over revenue-share terms. Allocation is all-or-nothing per surface and per term.
mechanism.payment_rule: TAC = max(s * R, G_amortised), where s is the contractual revenue share, R is the advertising revenue generated on that surface, and G is any non-cancelable guaranteed minimum. Google's own accounting policy states it exactly: 'To the extent we expect revenues generated under an arrangement to exceed the guaranteed minimum revenue share payments, we recognize traffic acquisition costs on a contractual revenue share basis... Otherwise, we recognize the guaranteed revenue share payments as traffic acquisition costs on a straight-line basis over the term.' Payment may also include equity (a warrant, or a direct stake).
mechanism.information_structure: Radically asymmetric. The search engine knows R per query, its own serving cost, and its rival's approximate yield; the access-point owner knows only what each bidder offers. Advertisers see none of it. The terms are private: the 2002 Google-AOL contract was never filed, and FOF para 298 of the 2024 opinion redacts the Apple revenue-share rate.
mechanism.risk_allocation: The guarantee is contingent on delivery, not on monetisation. Google's FY2004 10-K: 'if a Google Network member were unable to perform under the contract, such as being unable to provide search queries, as defined under the terms of that agreement, then the Company would not be obligated to make any non-cancelable guaranteed minimum revenue share payments to that member.' So a revenue guarantee is a floor on the partner's price per delivered query, not a bet on the buyer's own monetisation.
assumptions_added: Deal terms reported but never filed (the ~$100m guarantee and ~85% share) are treated as grade-B inputs and every conclusion that depends on them is tested for sensitivity.

AOL's share of Google's network revenue is inferred by dividing the disclosed AOL-share-of-total-revenue by disclosed network revenue; this assumes essentially all AOL-generated revenue was booked as network revenue, which the 10-K's wording ('primarily through our AdSense program') supports but does not guarantee.

Google's take rate on AOL specifically was never disclosed. Where an AOL-specific take rate is needed it is set at 15% (the complement of the reported 85% share) and marked illustrative, with the network-average take rate shown as an alternative.
Serving cost per syndicated impression is assumed to be at most proportional to revenue; a half-proportional allocation is carried as the alternative bound.

baseline.name: Counterfactual baseline: Overture's syndication network holds
baseline.why_this_baseline: No rival auction design is at issue here; the rival is a rival BALANCE SHEET running the same instruments. Overture's own FY2002 10-K describes the identical toolkit - 'fixed payments, based on a guaranteed minimum amount of traffic delivered, which often carry reciprocal performance guarantees from the affiliates', percentage-of-revenue payments, per-click, per-impression and per-search payments. The guarantee was not Google's invention. The counterfactual is therefore not 'what if nobody used guarantees' but 'what if the incumbent had been able to outbid'.

baseline_rules.allocation: Same: private negotiation for default placement on portals, browsers and metasearch sites.
baseline_rules.payment: Same instrument set. Overture's blended payout was 58% of revenue in 2002 (56% in 2001), guided to 63-64% by Q1 2003 and rising 0.25-0.50 points per quarter thereafter.
baseline_rules.structural_difference: Overture had almost no owned destination to cross-subsidise a bid. Google took 74.7% of its 2002 advertising revenue from inventory it did not have to pay for. That asymmetry, not the contract form, is what decided the AOL auction.

capture_attribution.question: Between 2002 and 2008, how much of Google's revenue growth is attributable to auction yield (revenue per query) versus distribution volume (queries bought)?
capture_attribution.verdict: BOUNDED, and against both simple stories. Distribution was decisive for the 2002-2004 beachhead and again after 2008; inside 2002-2008 the two engines were close to co-equal, with a documented tilt that depends on which ledger you read. On GROSS revenue growth, syndication supplied 31.9% and owned sites 68.1%. On NET-OF-TAC revenue, syndication supplied 9.4% of the 2008 total - the syndicated dollar bought position, not profit. Inside owned-site growth, a log decomposition splits 52-56% to query volume and 44-48% to yield per query, and that volume was overwhelmingly NOT bought: distribution TAC was 3.7% of owned-site revenue in 2007 and 4.5% in 2008. The defensible synthesis is causal rather than accounting: the auction set the budget for the distribution bid (only the higher-RPM bidder can afford an 85% share) and the distribution secured the query base the auction then monetised. Neither engine is sufficient; the yield engine is the binding constraint on the volume engine, which is why 'the better auction won' and 'the bigger cheque won' are the same sentence read from different ends.

breaks.name: A revenue guarantee is not a bet on your own monetisation
breaks.demonstration: X2 and the FY2004 10-K clause: 'if a Google Network member were unable to perform under the contract, such as being unable to provide search queries... then the Company would not be obligated to make any non-cancelable guaranteed minimum revenue share payments to that member.'
breaks.why_it_matters: Every popular retelling treats the ~$100m as money Google could have lost outright. It is closer to a floor price per delivered query, contingent on delivery, amortised over the term, and extinguished once cumulative revenue passes G/s. The bet-the-company framing survives only as a statement about the headline number.

breaks.name: The deal terms are unfalsifiable and the popular figures are grade B at best
breaks.demonstration: The May 2002 contract was never filed with the SEC. The ~$100m and ~85% figures trace to secondary accounts; the era-6 record already flags that the page reference in Battelle has not been captured and that the Search Engine Watch page previously cited contains no financial terms. FOF para 298 of the 2024 opinion redacts the analogous rate for Apple.
breaks.why_it_matters: The entire quantitative literature on this deal rests on two numbers nobody can check. X3 shows the accounts can bound them - the 91%/84% TAC ratios bracket the share and date the guarantee's expiry - but an analysis that quotes $100m without that reconstruction is quoting a rumour.

breaks.name: Equity is the expensive leg and nobody counts it
breaks.demonstration: X4: a warrant carried at $13.871m realised approximately $1,134.6m, 11.3x the cash guarantee, for 2.71% of the company.
breaks.why_it_matters: Distribution deals priced in equity look cheap at signature and cost most in exactly the states of the world where the buyer succeeds. This is a systematic mispricing, not a one-off: the payoff to the access-point owner is long the buyer's own success.

breaks.name: The take-rate ratchet reverses
breaks.demonstration: Google's network take rate rose 9% (2002) to 24.7% (2006), then FELL to 21.5% (2007) and 21.3% (2008). The FY2008 10-K attributes future increases in TAC to competition for members and to guaranteed-minimum members specifically.
breaks.why_it_matters: The margin on syndication is a function of competitive intensity for partners, not of mechanism design. Any simulator that treats the take rate as a designed parameter rather than an auction outcome will get the era's economics backwards.

breaks.name: The best justification for a 9% take rate is unmeasurable
breaks.demonstration: Syndication is usually defended on the ground that more inventory attracts more advertisers, which deepens the auction and raises CPCs on OWNED inventory. Google never disclosed advertiser counts, per-keyword auction depth, or owned-site CPCs, and the era-6 record's own advertiser-count claim is grade C with an interval spanning 550k to 2.6m.
breaks.why_it_matters: The load-bearing economic argument for the volume engine is an externality with no public measurement. It is stated here as a hypothesis with a simulator hook, never as a finding.

breaks.name: Syndication manufactures your future competitor
breaks.demonstration: Overture took ~60% of revenue from Microsoft- and Yahoo-supplied traffic; Yahoo bought Overture in July 2003 and Microsoft built adCenter. Google took 15-16% from AOL and later paid $1.0bn for 5% of it, losing $717m.
breaks.why_it_matters: The distribution partner learns the economics of the business it is renting out. The mechanism's stability depends on the partner not being able to integrate backwards - which is exactly what the access-point owners did next.

breaks.name: Under monopoly the default payment stops being a price and becomes a barrier
breaks.demonstration: The court found the challenged contracts covered roughly 50% of US general search queries, that Google's internal 2020 analysis projected a 60-80% iOS query loss without the Safari default, and separately that Google could raise text-ad prices 5% or more without losing substantial advertisers.
breaks.why_it_matters: This is the single most important caveat for the twin-engine story. Once distribution forecloses half the market, the yield engine's later gains cannot be attributed to auction design - the court found them attributable to power. The 2002-2008 yield story and the 2019-2024 yield story are different phenomena wearing the same name.

breaks.name: The remedy left the mechanism intact
breaks.demonstration: The September 2025 remedies opinion barred exclusive contracts and capped terms at one year, but declined to prohibit the payments or to order divestiture, reasoning that ending the payments would cripple downstream partners.
breaks.why_it_matters: A reader who takes the 2024 liability ruling as the end of the distribution engine will misread everything after it. What was outlawed was exclusivity, not the revenue share; the instrument that began with AOL in 2002 is still running.

breaks.name: Gross revenue recognition flatters the volume engine by construction
breaks.demonstration: Google's S-1 originally presented network revenue NET of TAC ($12.278m for 2002); the FY2004 10-K restates it gross ($103.937m). The same business is 24% of revenue on one basis and about 3% on the other.
breaks.why_it_matters: The famous '48.7% of revenue came from the network' statistic is an accounting-presentation artefact as much as an economic fact. Any capture-attribution argument that uses gross revenue shares without the net-of-TAC counterpart is measuring the presentation.

findings: The 2002 AOL guarantee was bet-the-company as a headline (1.16x prior-year revenue, 2.98x cash) and structurally bounded as an exposure (break-even at $117.6m of cumulative AOL revenue, cleared 2.55x by end-2003, void entirely if AOL failed to deliver queries). Claim 1 holds only in its headline form.

The filings corroborate the never-filed contract and date its expiry. AOL was 63.4% of Google's 2002 network revenue; the blended 91% TAC ratio sits three to six points above the reported 85% share, and the residual of $11.9-15.7m is the guarantee's realised first-year cost. The ratio's fall to 84% in 2003 is the guarantee going out of the money.

The instrument that actually cost Google money was equity. A warrant carried at $13.871m realised about $1,134.6m for AOL's parent - 11.3x the cash guarantee - for 2.71% of the company. Add the 2006 sequel ($1.0bn in, $283m out) and the AOL relationship is, on a pure investment basis, a loss.

Syndicated and owned advertising dollars are different businesses by roughly an order of magnitude: 4.5x apart on revenue retention in 2008 (95.5 cents against 21.3), 11x apart in 2002, and 5.3-9.2x apart on fully allocated gross margin. The take rate is not a margin.

The volume was still rational for three reasons, of which only two are provable: about $4.71bn of cumulative contribution on $59.07bn of era advertising revenue, and the foreclosure of the largest US access point from the incumbent. The third - that syndication deepened the auction and raised owned-site CPCs - has no public measurement and is recorded as a break.

The two engines are not rivals for causal credit. The maximum feasible distribution bid IS the yield net of serving cost, so the higher-RPM bidder wins the default by construction. The disclosed 33.4-point payout gap between Google's network (91%) and Overture's (58%) in 2002 is the observable signature.

Capture attribution, 2002-2008: syndication supplied 31.9% of gross advertising-revenue growth but 9.4% of 2008 revenue after revenue share; owned-site growth splits 52-56% volume against 44-48% yield; and only 3.7-4.5% of owned-site revenue was spent buying directed traffic. Distribution bought the beachhead, the auction bought the rest, and the pure-distribution thesis becomes correct only after the era ends.

The Mehta ruling prices the mature instrument at roughly half of all US search queries, 54% of search revenue on Google's own 2017 estimate, and $26.3bn a year - more than the $19.5bn cost of operating search and search ads. Applying the disclosed 36% Apple rate to the $20bn 2022 payment implies about $55.6bn of Safari-originated search advertising revenue, 34% of Google Search & other revenue.

The twin engines did not stay balanced. Alphabet's headline TAC rate is almost unchanged across twenty years (23.0% in 2002, 21.8% in 2022) but its composition inverted: distribution's share of TAC went from 11% (2008) to 58% (2021), a 40-fold rise in absolute spend. The volume engine ate the P&L after the auction era, not during it.

The court outlawed the exclusivity, not the payment. The September 2025 remedy left the revenue share running under one-year terms, which means the instrument first deployed against Overture in May 2002 is still the operating mechanism of search distribution in 2026.

twin_engine.thesis: Google's era-6 position was built by two engines that are usually told as one story and are not substitutes. The auction is the YIELD engine: it sets revenue per query. Distribution is the VOLUME engine: it buys the queries. Each engine's own analysis reaches the same boundary from opposite sides - the auction explains price and cannot explain volume; distribution explains volume and cannot pay for itself without the price.

yield_engine.mechanism: AdWords Select, February 2002: rank by bid x predicted click-through rate, charge the minimum needed to hold position, quality-adjusted, per click.
yield_engine.what_it_sets: revenue per query (RPM), and the ranking of who gets seen
load_bearing_results: Pure-bid ranking mis-orders by expected revenue exactly when 1 < b_i/b_j < q_j/q_i (finding f1).
At fixed bids, quality weighting raises revenue and clicks together: $28.18 to $52.58 per 1000 impressions and 18 to 58 clicks (f2).
The gain is VOLUME, not price - average price per click falls 42%, from $1.57 to $0.91 (f3). Every retelling that says quality weighting let Google charge more has the sign backwards.
GSP is not truthful, so its revenue is a band of [$440, $760] - a factor of 1.727 - whose position is set by advertiser sophistication rather than by the mechanism (f6, f7).
First price with equilibrium shading is revenue-equivalent to second price for every n, so the 2019 DISPLAY switch contains no yield mechanism (f8, f10).

Every decisive parameter - predicted CTR, the quality-based reserve, the squashing exponent, the format multiplier, the click-validity test - was computed by the seller and unaudited; no industry click-measurement standard existed until 2009 (f15).
yield_engine.what_it_cannot_explain: Query volume. Overture ran the pure-bid design and still led paid-search revenue through 2002 ($667.7m against Google's $439.5m of total revenue), and Yahoo did not adopt quality weighting until Panama on 5 February 2007, long after the distribution war was settled. The auction engine states this itself as finding f14 and directs the reader to the distribution engine.

volume_engine.mechanism: Revenue-share syndication with minimum-revenue guarantees and default placement: TAC = max(s * R, G_amortised), sometimes paid in equity.
volume_engine.what_it_sets: how many queries reach the auction at all
load_bearing_results: The May 2002 AOL agreement was bet-the-company on the headline (1.16x prior-year revenue, 2.98x cash) and structurally bounded as an exposure - break-even at $117.6m of cumulative AOL revenue, cleared 2.55x by end-2003, void entirely if AOL failed to deliver queries.
The instrument that actually cost money was equity: a warrant carried at $13.871m realised about $1,134.6m, 11.3x the cash guarantee, for 2.71% of the company.
Syndicated and owned dollars are different businesses: 4.48x apart on retention in 2008, 11x in 2002, 5.3-9.2x apart on fully allocated gross margin.
The network peaked at 48.7% of total revenue in 2004 but only 9.4% of 2008 advertising revenue net of TAC. The syndication engine bought position, not profit.
The take-rate ratchet reverses: 9% (2002) to 24.7% (2006), then back to 21.5% (2007) and 21.3% (2008). Take rate is an auction outcome, not a design parameter (break B4).
By 2021 the same instrument was $26.3bn a year and 57.7% of all TAC, was held illegal in 2024, and survived the September 2025 remedy with only its exclusivity struck out.
volume_engine.what_it_cannot_explain: Why Google could win the bid. The maximum feasible distribution bid IS the yield net of serving cost, so a firm with lower RPM cannot outbid regardless of contract design (example X8).

twin_engine.how_the_engines_couple: The coupling is a budget constraint, and both analyses derive it independently. The distribution engine's X8 shows the maximum feasible bid for a default equals revenue per query minus serving cost, so only the higher-RPM bidder can afford an 85% share - and the disclosed 33.4-point payout gap in 2002 (Google's network at 91% of network advertising revenue against Overture's blended 58%) is the observable signature. The auction engine's f14 reaches the same junction from the other side: the auction explains yield per query and not query volume. The chapters should therefore run them as one sentence read from two ends - 'the better auction won' and 'the bigger cheque won' describe the same event, because the auction set the size of the cheque.
twin_engine.asymmetry_that_decided_it: Not the contract form. Overture's own FY2002 10-K describes the identical instrument set - guaranteed minimums with reciprocal performance guarantees, percentage-of-revenue, per-click, per-impression payments. What Google had and Overture did not was an owned destination carrying no revenue share: 74.7% of Google's 2002 advertising revenue came from inventory it did not have to pay for. That cross-subsidy, funded by yield, is what the volume engine spent.

death_coda.summary: Era 7 kills the auction as the price-setter on both sides at once, and the two engines record different halves of the death.
death_coda.yield_side: Header bidding (2014-15) forced the display exchange to a unified first price on 2019-09-05 - a transparency change with no yield mechanism behind it - while SEARCH went the other way, to rGSP plus squashing and format pricing, all seller-set, none opt-outable. The auction did not have to be replaced to become a price-setting instrument; it only had to be tuned, because GSP's own equilibrium band was already 73% wide (findings f10, f11, f12, f13).
death_coda.volume_side: The same distribution instrument scaled 40-fold and inverted in composition - distribution TAC went from 11% of all TAC in 2008 to 58% in 2021 - was found illegal in August 2024, and then survived: the September 2025 remedy barred exclusivity and capped terms at one year while leaving the payments in place (breaks B7, B8).
death_coda.reader_warning: Do not merge the two 2019 changes. Display went first-price; search never did. This is the most common factual error in retellings of 2019 and both engines flag it.

capture_attribution.question: Between 2002 and 2008, how much of Google's revenue growth is attributable to auction yield (revenue per query) versus distribution volume (queries bought)?
capture_attribution.verdict_verbatim: BOUNDED, and against both simple stories. Distribution was decisive for the 2002-2004 beachhead and again after 2008; inside 2002-2008 the two engines were close to co-equal, with a documented tilt that depends on which ledger you read. On GROSS revenue growth, syndication supplied 31.9% and owned sites 68.1%. On NET-OF-TAC revenue, syndication supplied 9.4% of the 2008 total - the syndicated dollar bought position, not profit. Inside owned-site growth, a log decomposition splits 52-56% to query volume and 44-48% to yield per query, and that volume was overwhelmingly NOT bought: distribution TAC was 3.7% of owned-site revenue in 2007 and 4.5% in 2008. The defensible synthesis is causal rather than accounting: the auction set the budget for the distribution bid (only the higher-RPM bidder can afford an 85% share) and the distribution secured the query base the auction then monetised. Neither engine is sufficient; the yield engine is the binding constraint on the volume engine, which is why 'the better auction won' and 'the bigger cheque won' are the same sentence read from different ends.
capture_attribution.one_line: BOUNDED and against both simple stories: inside 2002-2008 the engines are close to co-equal - syndication supplied 31.9% of gross advertising-revenue growth but only 9.4% of 2008 revenue net of TAC, and owned-site growth splits 52-56% volume against 44-48% yield on volume that was 94-97% unbought - so distribution bought the beachhead and the auction converted it; the pure-distribution thesis becomes correct only after the era, once defaults take 58% of TAC.
capture_attribution.auction_side_concurrence: engines.auction.findings f14 ('attribution caveat'): the auction analysis explicitly declines to claim the design caused the capture, on the grounds that Overture led paid-search revenue through 2002 with the crude design and Yahoo waited until 2007 to copy the better one. Nothing in the auction engine claims a share of the growth; the attribution is the distribution engine's alone, and the two are consistent.
capture_attribution.weakest_link: mech-capture-002 is grade C and inherits two grade-C query denominators from the era-6 record. The volume/yield split is a band, not a point, and the chapters must carry it as 52-56% against 44-48%, never as 54% flat.
capture_attribution.boundary_condition: Break B7 is the binding caveat on the whole twin-engine frame: once the defaults foreclose roughly half the market, later yield gains cannot be attributed to auction design - the court attributed them to power. The 2002-2008 yield story and the 2019-2024 yield story are different phenomena wearing the same name, and era-7 evidence must not be used to attribute era-6 growth (the same discount the distribution engine applies to weight W5).

open_tensions.subject: Is the 2019 pricing power continuous with the 2005 mechanism, or a different phenomenon?
open_tensions.auction_position: Continuity. Finding f13 and break-2: from August 2005 the Quality-Score-derived minimum bid was a seller-set price, and on a one-bidder query the reserve IS the price - a $0.01-to-$1.00 move is a 100x revenue change with one advertiser and no change to anything the user sees. 'The DOJ-era pricing knobs are not a break with the 2002-2008 mechanism. They are the same lever, on a bigger base, with a trial transcript attached.'
open_tensions.distribution_position: Discontinuity. Break B7: once the defaults foreclosed roughly half the market, the court attributed the yield gains to power rather than design. 'The 2002-2008 yield story and the 2019-2024 yield story are different phenomena wearing the same name.'
open_tensions.is_this_a_contradiction: No. They are claims about different objects - the auction says the INSTRUMENT is continuous, the distribution says the CAUSAL ATTRIBUTION of the gains is not. Both can hold: the same lever can be lawful pricing in 2005 and an exercise of monopoly power in 2019 without the lever changing.
open_tensions.instruction_to_chapters: Carry both, explicitly, in that order: the lever is old, the power behind it is new. Do not present either engine as correcting the other, and do not collapse the pair into a single sentence.

open_tensions.subject: The strongest economic justification for a 9% take rate is unmeasurable.
open_tensions.position: The distribution engine's break B5 records the syndication-deepens-the-auction externality as a hypothesis with no public measurement. It is exactly the channel that would let the volume engine raise the yield engine's prices, which is the one coupling this merge cannot quantify in either direction.
open_tensions.instruction_to_chapters: State it as an open question with a simulator hook, never as a finding. It is also the honest limit of the capture-attribution verdict.

open_tensions.subject: The rGSP-versus-format-pricing accounting does not close.
open_tensions.position: The auction engine's own open_tension: the record says rGSP replaced format pricing because it made more money, yet format pricing was about 20% of text-ads RPM while rGSP's disclosed persistent effect was +5.74%. Either the 20% was not all incremental or the two knobs were substitutes on the same surplus.
open_tensions.instruction_to_chapters: Preserved unresolved. The record as summarised does not settle it and neither engine asserts a resolution.
